channel.title: Index UK
channel.description: Briefings and places for England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

item.title: How the kingdom is actually arranged
item.description: Four nations, three devolved legislatures, a shared crown, and a set of neighbours that are not in the United Kingdom at all.

item.title: A first week that leaves London
item.description: Seven days, one base in the capital and one beyond it, for someone who wants the country rather than a checklist of queues.

item.title: The railway, without the folklore
item.description: How to buy a ticket, which names matter, and why the 09:12 is a better idea than a hire car for most first journeys.

item.title: Parliament, the Crown, and who decides what
item.description: A short civic map: Westminster, Holyrood, the Senedd, Stormont, and a monarchy that reigns more than it rules.

item.title: Weather, coast, and when to go
item.description: A maritime climate with no guaranteed season, a west that is wetter, and a calendar that belongs to schools as much as to weather.

item.title: Eating in four nations
item.description: Not a apology for the food, and not a list of themed pubs. What people actually sit down to, and where a visitor should aim.

item.title: Free museums, and what they are for
item.description: General admission is still free at the great national collections. That is a civic fact, not a loophole, and it changes how you should spend a rainy day.

item.title: National parks, a working index
item.description: Fifteen national parks, none of them a wilderness in the American sense, all of them lived-in landscapes with gates, farms and weather.

item.title: London without the queue
item.description: A capital that rewards a neighbourhood, a river and a refusal to see everything. Four days is a good start. Four hours per museum is a mistake.

item.title: Scotland north of Edinburgh
item.description: Edinburgh is the front door, not the house. How far to go, how not to drive it in a blur, and what the Highlands actually feel like.

item.title: Wales, in the language of the place
item.description: A country of three million with its own parliament, a living Celtic language, a coal-and-choir past, and a coast that keeps going.

item.title: Northern Ireland for a long weekend
item.description: Belfast, the coast, and a history that is not a theme. How to spend four days without pretending the Troubles were a postcard.

item.title: Walking rights, and three classic routes
item.description: Where you may put your feet, what a right of way is, and three walks that explain more than a viewpoint car park.

item.title: Sunday, pubs, and the shape of a day
item.description: Opening hours, the difference between a pub and a bar, and why Monday morning is a bad time to discover a town.

item.title: London
item.description: A dozen towns that share a river and a transport card. Greater London, England.

item.title: Edinburgh
item.description: A capital on a ridge, with a rational city at its feet. Lothian, Scotland.

item.title: Bath
item.description: Roman water under a Georgian stage set. Somerset, England.

item.title: York
item.description: Walls, snickelways, and a railway city that still feels medieval after dark. North Yorkshire, England.

item.title: The Lake District
item.description: Fells, water, and a holiday geography that fills up in July. Cumbria, England.

item.title: The Cotswolds
item.description: Limestone villages, long views, and a coach circuit that is easy to outwalk. Gloucestershire and neighbours, England.

item.title: Cornwall
item.description: A long county of coves, pasties and a summer traffic problem. Cornwall, England.

item.title: Isle of Skye
item.description: Black rock, changing water, and an island that punishes a one-night stand. Inner Hebrides, Scotland.

item.title: Cardiff
item.description: A capital on a human scale, with a castle in the middle and the sea at the end of the street. South Wales, Wales.

item.title: Belfast
item.description: A red-brick port with a short memory in the stones and a long one in the people. County Antrim, Northern Ireland.

item.title: Liverpool
item.description: A maritime city with museums that punch above, and a sense of humour that gets there first. Merseyside, England.

item.title: Eryri
item.description: Snowdonia by its Welsh name: slate, sharp hills, and towns that exist for more than the car park. Gwynedd, Wales.

item.title: Oxford
item.description: A working city that happens to be built of colleges. Oxfordshire, England.

item.title: Cambridge
item.description: King’s College, the Backs, and a river that is not the whole university. Cambridgeshire, England.

item.title: Windsor
item.description: The largest castle in the world still used as a house, and a town that knows it. Berkshire, England.

item.title: Durham
item.description: A cathedral and a castle on a river peninsula, and one of the great small cities of the north. County Durham, England.

item.title: Glasgow
item.description: Scotland’s larger city: sandstone, museums, and a humour that does not wait to be asked. Greater Glasgow, Scotland.

item.title: St Andrews
item.description: A ruined cathedral, an old university, and the golf that the town has decided to be famous for. Fife, Scotland.

item.title: Whitby
item.description: An abbey on a cliff, a harbour full of boats, and a town that earns its fish and chips. North Yorkshire, England.

item.title: Conwy
item.description: A complete medieval town wall, a castle in the water, and a bridge that used to be the wonder. North Wales, Wales.

item.title: The Peak District
item.description: England’s first national park: gritstone edges, limestone dales, and cities close enough to fill the car parks. Derbyshire and neighbours, England.

item.title: Dover
item.description: The white cliffs, a harbour that faces France, and the shortest serious statement of the island. Kent, England.

item.title: Glenfinnan
item.description: A viaduct, a loch, and the monument where the Jacobite rising was raised. The Highlands, Scotland.

item.title: Canterbury
item.description: A cathedral city an hour from London, with a wall you can still walk and a high street you can ignore. Kent, England.

item.title: Brighton
item.description: A regency seafront, a pavilion that looks like a dare, and a city that does not behave like a resort. East Sussex, England.

item.title: Bristol
item.description: A harbour city with a bridge that still looks impossible, and a centre that is not a museum of itself. Bristol, England.

item.title: Chester
item.description: A Roman grid, a complete city wall, and the Rows: galleries of shops above the street. Cheshire, England.

item.title: Manchester
item.description: A red-brick capital of the north, with serious museums and a centre that expects you to have plans after dark. Greater Manchester, England.

item.title: Inverness
item.description: The town at the top of the Great Glen, more useful than it is famous, and the right night before the north. The Highlands, Scotland.

item.title: St Davids
item.description: Britain’s smallest city: a cathedral in a hollow, and a coast path that is the real reason to come. Pembrokeshire, Wales.

item.title: Hadrian’s Wall
item.description: The stone edge of a Roman province, still walking the crags between Newcastle and Carlisle. Northumberland, England.

item.title: Salisbury
item.description: A cathedral close, a famous spire, and the sensible base for Stonehenge if the stones are actually the point. Wiltshire, England.
